activities.title: Practical Context: Postal Service Standardized Shipping Parcel Sizing

analogy.headline: Practical Context: Postal Service Standardized Shipping Parcel Sizing
analogy.story:
A postal package sorting center sorts packages using an intrinsic physical metric: volumetric weight. Every parcel possesses an innate weight and dimensions stamped onto its shipping label.

When two parcels meet on a sorting conveyor diverter, the mechanism asks: 'Is Parcel A heavier than Parcel B?' A parcel inherently knows how to measure itself against another parcel of the same specification (natural ordering).

The `Comparable` interface models this exact intrinsic capability: an object knows its own natural rank when lined up alongside peers of its own kind.
analogy.keyTakeaway: Comparable defines the single intrinsic natural order for a class. Implementing it enables automatic sorting in Arrays.sort(), Collections.sort(), and TreeSet.

activities.title: The compareTo() Contract, Mathematical Axioms & equals() Consistency

keyTakeaways: Comparable<T> requires implementing int compareTo(T o)
Returns negative if this < o; zero if this equals o; positive if this > o
Must satisfy antisymmetry, transitivity, and congruence axioms
TreeSet and TreeMap use compareTo() for uniqueness, NOT equals()!

activities.content:
### The java.lang.Comparable Interface

The **`java.lang.Comparable<T>`** interface imposes a total ordering on the objects of each class that implements it. This ordering is referred to as the class's **natural ordering**:
```java
package java.lang;

public interface Comparable<T> {
    int compareTo(T o);
}
```
Classes like `String`, `Integer`, `Double`, `LocalDate`, and `BigDecimal` all implement `Comparable<T>`.

---

### The Three-Way Return Sign Contract

The method `compareTo(T other)` compares this object with the specified object for order:
* Returns a **negative integer** if `this < other`.
* Returns **zero (`0`)** if `this` is considered equal in ordering to `other`.
* Returns a **positive integer** if `this > other`.
* Throws `NullPointerException` if `other` is `null` (natural comparison with null is forbidden).

---

### Mathematical Ordering Axioms

To prevent erratic sorting failures and infinite re-balancing loops in `TreeSet`/`TreeMap`, `compareTo()` must strictly adhere to three mathematical laws:
1. **Antisymmetry**: `sgn(x.compareTo(y)) == -sgn(y.compareTo(x))` for all `x` and `y`.
2. **Transitivity**: If `x.compareTo(y) > 0` and `y.compareTo(z) > 0`, then `x.compareTo(z) > 0`.
3. **Congruence**: If `x.compareTo(y) == 0`, then `sgn(x.compareTo(z)) == sgn(y.compareTo(z))` for all `z`.

---

### Consistency with equals() and the TreeSet Dilemma

It is strongly recommended that **`(x.compareTo(y) == 0) == (x.equals(y))`**. If a class violates this recommendation, collections like `TreeSet` and `TreeMap` will violate the general `Set` / `Map` interface contract!

**The Infamous BigDecimal Trap**:
```java
BigDecimal b1 = new BigDecimal("2.0");
BigDecimal b2 = new BigDecimal("2.00");

System.out.println(b1.equals(b2));       // false (different scale: 1 vs 2)
System.out.println(b1.compareTo(b2));    // 0     (identical numerical value!)

Set<BigDecimal> hashSet = new HashSet<>();
hashSet.add(b1); hashSet.add(b2);
System.out.println(hashSet.size());      // 2 (HashSet uses equals())

Set<BigDecimal> treeSet = new TreeSet<>();
treeSet.add(b1); treeSet.add(b2);
System.out.println(treeSet.size());      // 1 (TreeSet uses compareTo() == 0!)
```

---

### Executable Demonstration: Domain Natural Ordering with Safe Comparisons

activities.title: Multi-Attribute Version Number Natural Sorter
activities.description: Trace a Semantic Versioning (SemVer) class implementing Comparable across major, minor, and patch numbers.

steps.description: Compare major version first using Integer.compare(). If non-zero, return immediately.
If major versions are equal, fall through to compare minor, then patch.

questions.question: What happens if a class's compareTo() method violates the transitivity law (a > b and b > c, but a < c)?
options: The compiler catches the violation at build-time
Sorting algorithms like TimSort may crash at runtime with an IllegalArgumentException: Comparison method violates its general contract!
The JVM falls back to sorting by hashCode
questions.explanation: Java's sorting algorithm (TimSort) verifies ordering invariants during its merge steps. If a comparator or compareTo violates transitivity or antisymmetry, TimSort throws an IllegalArgumentException: Comparison method violates its general contract!

questions.question: Why does adding new BigDecimal("2.0") and new BigDecimal("2.00") to a TreeSet result in a set of size 1?
options: Because TreeSet removes duplicates by calling hashCode()
Because TreeSet determines element uniqueness using compareTo() == 0 rather than equals()
Because the second element is rejected as invalid input
questions.explanation: TreeSet is a NavigableSet based on a Red-Black tree. It determines duplicate elements strictly by testing if compareTo(a, b) == 0. Because 2.0 and 2.00 are numerically equal (compareTo returns 0), TreeSet treats them as duplicates even though equals() returns false.

activities.title: Senior Engineer Interview: Comparable vs Comparator

qaList.question: When should you implement Comparable<T> on a domain entity versus defining an external Comparator<T>?
qaList.answer:
Implement 'Comparable<T>' when an entity has a single, obvious, uncontroversial 'natural' ordering that applies in 90% of use cases (e.g., Integer by numeric value, LocalDate by chronological date, Employee by employee ID). It modifies the class itself.

Use an external 'Comparator<T>' when: 1. You need secondary or situational orderings (e.g., sort employees by salary, by last name, or by department). 2. You do not own the source code of the class and cannot modify it to implement Comparable. 3. You want to parameterize sorting strategies at runtime (e.g., user selects 'Sort by Price: Low to High' on an e-commerce catalog). Comparator decouples the sorting strategy from the entity.

activities.title: Self-Evaluation Checklist
checklist: I understand the 3-way return sign contract of compareTo()
I know the three mathematical axioms: antisymmetry, transitivity, congruence
I understand why consistency between compareTo() and equals() is critical for TreeSet
I always use Integer.compare() and Double.compare() instead of subtraction

practiceProblems.title: Student Natural Order: GPA Descending, ID Ascending

practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement Comparable<Transaction> for class Transaction(String id, long timestamp, double amount) sorting chronologically by timestamp ascending.

practiceProblems.title: Product SKU Lexicographical Natural Order
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement Comparable<Product> for class Product(String sku, double price) where natural order sorts lexicographically by sku ascending.

practiceProblems.title: Audit compareTo Consistency with equals
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement a generic method boolean isConsistentWithEquals(T a, T b) for <T extends Comparable<T>> that returns true if (a.compareTo(b) == 0) == a.equals(b).

practiceProblems.title: Comparable Boundary Clamper
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement a method clampComparable(T val, T lower, T upper) for <T extends Comparable<T>> that returns lower if val < lower, upper if val > upper, and val otherwise.
